idiom_name: public static factory methods on the type (TimeSpan.FromSeconds, Guid.NewGuid)
implementation_notes: The .NET design guidelines say to prefer constructors and to add a static factory when the operation's semantics do not map to construction (Parse/From/Open/Create), so the named creation methods sit on the type itself or in a dedicated static factory type (File.Create returns a FileStream). Because C# generates a public parameterless constructor whenever none is declared, making the factory the only route requires an explicit private constructor - which then also closes the type to subclassing and to serializer materialization unless a constructor is deliberately exposed. Records and object initializers already give simple data types a language-level named construction form, so keep factories for validation, conversion, caching and subtype choice.
pitfalls: A private constructor blocks System.Text.Json and ORM materialization: serializers need an accessible constructor (or a [JsonConstructor] marker), otherwise the type cannot be deserialized at all.
Static factories hide cost: a method named Create or Load that performs I/O reads like a cheap conversion at the call site - name it for the work it does and make the failure mode explicit.
Static factories cannot be overridden and a sealed type with a private constructor cannot be subclassed; if tests or frameworks must substitute creation, inject an IFactory or delegate instead.
